---
title: "Julia core"
---

With the term "core", we mean the computational engine of Ribasim. As detailed in the
[usage](/reference/usage.qmd) documentation, it is generally used as a command line tool.

A quick overview of the model concept is available in the [introduction](/concept/concept.qmd#sec-concept), while a more in-depth discussion is available on the [model concept](/concept/modelconcept.qmd) page.
The theory is described on the [equations](/concept/equations.qmd) page, and more in-depth numerical considerations are described on the [numerical considerations](/concept/numerics.qmd) page. As allocation is a large and self-contained part of the Ribasim core, it is described on the separate [allocation](/concept/allocation.qmd) page. Input validation is described on the [validation](/reference/validation.qmd) page.

The core is implemented in the [Julia programming language](https://julialang.org/), and
can be found in the [Ribasim repository](https://github.com/Deltares/Ribasim) under the
`core/` folder. For developers we also advise to read the
[developer documentation](/dev/core.qmd). Information on coupling can be found [here](/guide/coupling.qmd).

An overview of all components is given in the [installation](/getting-started/install.qmd#sec-components) section.

# The simulation loop {#sec-simulationloop}

The computational process can be divided into three phases:

- Model initialization
- Running the simulation loop
- Writing the output files

The figure below gives a more detailed description of the simulation loop in the form of a [sequence diagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequence_diagram). From top to bottom, it contains the following blocks:

- Allocation optimization; activated when the allocation timestep has been passed;
- Control actions; activated when some discrete control callback is triggered;
- Water balance; computing the flows over flow links happens each timestep;
- Time integration step; done by the integrator from `OrdinaryDiffEq.jl`.

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Int as Process: Integrator
    participant Optim as Process: Allocation optimization
    participant Param as Data: Parameters
    participant State as Data: State
    participant Sim as Process: Water balance
    loop Simulation loop (OrdinaryDiffEq.jl)
        activate Int
        %% Allocation
        rect rgb(200, 200, 200)
            opt Allocation optimization, per allocation network (JuMP.jl, HiGHS)
                activate Optim
                Int->>Optim: Callback: allocation timestep has passed
                Param-->>Optim: Input
                State-->>Optim: Input
                Optim->>Optim: Optimize Basin allocations if below target level
                Optim->>Optim: Optimize UserDemand allocation, per priority
                Optim-->>Param: Set allocated flow rates
                deactivate Optim
            end
        end
        %% Control
        rect rgb(200, 200, 200)
            opt Control actions
                Int->>Int: DiscreteControl callback
                Int-->>Param: Parameter updates by control
            end
        end
        %% water_balance!
        rect rgb(200, 200, 200)
            activate Sim
            State-->>Sim: Input
            Param-->>Sim: Input
            Sim->>Sim: Compute flows over links per node type
            Sim-->>Param: Set flows
            deactivate Sim
        end
        %% Time integration
        rect rgb(200, 200, 200)
            State-->>Int: Input
            Param-->>Int: Input
            Int->>Int: Time integration step
            Int-->>State: Update state
        end
        deactivate Int
  end
```

# Nested allocation {#sec-nested-allocation}

Since water systems may be extensive, like in the Netherlands, Ribasim models may become large networks with over ten thousand nodes.
To maintain a properly functioning allocation concept under these circumstances, the modeler can decompose the network domain into a primary network and multiple sub-networks.
The allocation will then be conducted in three steps:

1. conduct an inventory of demands from the sub-networks to inlets from the primary network,
2. allocate the available water in the primary network to the subnetwork inlets,
3. allocate the assigned water within each subnetwork to the individual demand nodes.

The demand nodes will then request this updated demand from the rule-based simulation.
Whether this updated demand is indeed abstracted depends on all the control mechanisms implemented in the rule-based simulation.

The following sequence diagram illustrates this calculation process within the allocation phase.

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
participant boundary
participant basin
participant user_demand
participant allocation_subNetwork
participant allocation_mainNetwork

user_demand->>allocation_subNetwork: demand
loop
   allocation_subNetwork-->>allocation_mainNetwork: demand inventory at inlets
end
user_demand->>allocation_mainNetwork: demand
boundary->>allocation_mainNetwork: source availability
basin->>allocation_mainNetwork: source availability
allocation_mainNetwork-->>allocation_mainNetwork: allocate to inlets (and user_demands)
allocation_mainNetwork->>user_demand: allocated
allocation_mainNetwork->>allocation_subNetwork: allocated
loop
   allocation_subNetwork-->>allocation_subNetwork: allocate to user_demands
end
allocation_subNetwork->>user_demand: allocated
user_demand->>basin: abstracted
```

# Substance (tracer) concentrations

::: {.callout-caution}
This is an unsupported experimental feature and is disabled by default.
We advise to use the [Delwaq coupling](/guide/coupling.qmd#sec-waterquality) for tracer calculations.
If you're interested in using this experimental feature, please [contact us](/contact.qmd).
:::

Ribasim can calculate concentrations of conservative tracers (i.e. substances that are non-reactive).
It does so after each timestep, using the flows of that timestep.

## Governing equation

Each Basin is instantaneously mixed, so water leaves a Basin with the concentration of that Basin.
This gives the mass balance of a substance in Basin $i$, with storage $S_i$ and concentration $C_i$:

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} \left( S_i C_i \right) = \sum_j q_{ji} C_j - q_{\text{out},i} C_i + f_i,
$$ {#eq-tracer-ode}

where $q_{ji} \geq 0$ is the flow from Basin $j$ to Basin $i$, $q_{\text{out},i}$ is the total outflow of Basin $i$, and $f_i$ is the mass per second from all other sources: boundaries, Basin forcings, loads and UserDemand return flows.
The flows come from the water balance, and are not affected by the concentrations other than through control.

Integrating @eq-tracer-ode over a timestep from $t_n$ to $t_{n+1}$ gives

$$
S_i^{n+1} C_i^{n+1} - S_i^n C_i^n = \sum_j \int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}} q_{ji} C_j \,\text{d}t - \int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}} q_{\text{out},i} C_i \,\text{d}t + F_i,
$$

where the superscripts denote the time and $F_i$ is the mass from the other sources over the timestep.

## Numerical scheme

How the integrals over the flows are approximated determines the numerical scheme.
The water balance gives the volumes $V_{ji}$ and $V_{\text{out},i}$ that flowed over the timestep.
Ribasim combines these with one concentration per Basin for the entire timestep, a weighted average of its concentrations at the start and the end of the timestep:

$$
\int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}} q_{ji} C_j \,\text{d}t \approx V_{ji} \left( \theta_j C_j^{n+1} + (1 - \theta_j) C_j^n \right).
$$

Using this for all flows and moving the unknown concentrations to the left hand side gives a linear system for the concentrations of all Basins at the end of the timestep:

$$
\left( S_i^{n+1} + \theta_i V_{\text{out},i} \right) C_i^{n+1} - \sum_j \theta_j V_{ji} C_j^{n+1} =
\left( S_i^n - (1 - \theta_i) V_{\text{out},i} \right) C_i^n + \sum_j (1 - \theta_j) V_{ji} C_j^n + F_i.
$$ {#eq-tracer-scheme}

The weights that Ribasim uses are determined per Basin and per timestep:

$$
\theta_i = \max\left( \frac{1}{2}, 1 - \frac{S_i^n}{V_{\text{out},i}} \right).
$$

The weight is $\theta_i = 1/2$ wherever possible, as this is the trapezoidal rule, which is second order accurate.
The concentrations can however only be guaranteed to stay non-negative if the coefficient of $C_i^n$ in @eq-tracer-scheme is non-negative, which requires $\theta_i \geq 1 - S_i^n / V_{\text{out},i}$.
So where more water flows out of a Basin within one timestep than twice its storage, the weight increases towards 1, using the smallest value that keeps the concentrations non-negative.

With these weights the matrix of @eq-tracer-scheme has non-positive off-diagonal entries and is strictly diagonally dominant by column, since a Basin keeps a small positive storage.
The system therefore always has a unique and non-negative solution, regardless of the size of the timestep.
The mass that leaves one Basin over a flow is the mass that enters the other, so the scheme conserves mass, and a substance can travel through any number of Basins within one timestep.
All substances share the same sparse matrix, which is factorized once per timestep.

If all Basins would use the same weight, the scheme reduces to these well known methods:

| $\theta$ | Method | Delwaq scheme | Properties |
|----------|--------|---------------|------------|
| $0$ | Forward Euler (explicit upwind) | 1 | First order. Needs no linear system. Non-negative if $V_{\text{out},i} \leq S_i^n$. A substance travels at most one Basin per timestep. |
| $1/2$ | Trapezoidal rule (Crank-Nicolson) | | Second order. Non-negative if $V_{\text{out},i} \leq 2 S_i^n$. |
| $1$ | Backward Euler (implicit upwind) | 15 | First order, with more numerical dispersion. Non-negative for any timestep. |

The [Delwaq coupling](/guide/coupling.qmd#sec-waterquality) uses scheme 15.
Adjusting the weight per Basin is also the idea of the local-theta schemes 21 and 22 of Delwaq, which however use $\theta_i = 0$ wherever that is stable, and limit the fluxes to avoid new extremes.
With instantaneously mixed Basins $\theta_i = 1/2$ is more accurate, since an explicit step in which the full storage of a Basin flows out moves all of its water to the next Basin without mixing.

The ResidenceTime tracer has the integral of the storage over the timestep as a source in $F_i$, which also uses the trapezoidal rule.
The UserDemand return flows are part of $F_i$ as well, with the concentrations of the Basins they came from at the start of the timestep.
So are the flows that reach a Basin via [Junction](/reference/node/junction.qmd#tracers) nodes that divide the flow: with the concentrations at the start of the timestep, so unlike the outflow of the Basin they came from, which is part of $V_{\text{out},i}$, this transport is explicit and does not conserve mass exactly.

We thus keep track of both mass and concentration of substances for each Basin.
Note that we have not added the substance mass to the states.
Only the volume of a flow over a timestep is used, in its net direction, so effectively flows are constant over a timestep.
The concentrations and loads from the input are constant over a timestep as well, since the solver stops at each time they change, so a pulse in one of these is followed exactly.

By default the following source tracers are enabled.

- Continuity (mass balance, fraction of all water sources, sum of all other source tracers)
- Initial (fraction of initial storages)
- LevelBoundary, FlowBoundary, UserDemand, Drainage, Precipitation (fraction of different boundaries)
- ResidenceTime (the average residence time of a water body in seconds)
